summary: Defines a minimal schema to support PKIX in an LDAPv2 environment, specifying only PKIX-specific components, as used with RFC 2559. It was replaced by RFC 4523.

eli5.summary: This defines the labels and drawers for storing digital ID cards in a directory, so everybody files them the same way.

questions: how to store x.509 certificates in ldap
where are certs revoked in ldap
subtitle: How to organize and store X.509 digital certificates in an LDAP directory.

tldr.problem: The X.509 public key infrastructure needs a place to store and retrieve certificates, and organizations want to use LDAP directories for this. But LDAP needs a schema that defines how to organize PKI objects.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a minimal LDAP schema with object classes and attributes for storing X.509 certificates, certificate revocation lists, and related PKI information in an LDAPv2 directory.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now use LDAP as a standard repository for digital certificates and CRLs, but this RFC was replaced by RFC 4523 with improvements and LDAPv3 support.

today: RFC 2587 is a Proposed Standard. It was replaced by RFC 4523, which provides a more comprehensive LDAP schema for PKIX and supports LDAPv3 in addition to LDAPv2.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2587 defines a schema for storing PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) objects in an LDAP directory. The schema is designed to be minimal, including only components needed for the X.509 PKI standard as used in RFC 2559, the LDAP access method for PKIX repositories.

LDAP directory entries can represent many types of objects. This RFC specifies auxiliary object classes and attributes that LDAP servers can add to existing entries to support PKI operations. LDAP clients can then query, add, modify and delete PKI information using these standard definitions.
sections.eli5: An LDAP directory is like a big phone book. This defines what extra fields you add to entries when you want to store certificates there.

sections.title: End Entities and Certification Authorities
sections.content:
The schema defines two main types of PKI objects:

End Entities are subjects of certificates (people, servers, or other things). The auxiliary object class pkiUser can be added to a directory entry representing an end entity. It allows the userCertificate attribute, which holds one or more X.509 certificates issued to that entity.

Certification Authorities issue certificates and maintain certificate revocation information. The auxiliary object class pkiCA can be added to entries representing CAs. It allows attributes for storing certificates issued to the CA, cross-certificates from other CAs, and both full and delta certificate revocation lists (CRLs).

The schema distinguishes between self-issued certificates (stored in cACertificate) and certificates from other realms (stored in crossCertificatePair).
sections.eli5: A person's entry can have their digital ID cards. A CA's entry can have its own cards and a blacklist of revoked cards from other places.

sections.title: Certificate and CRL Distribution
sections.content:
For CAs that publish certificate revocation lists, the RFC defines the cRLDistributionPoint object class. This is a directory entry that acts as a collection point for CRLs. It can hold a full CRL, delta CRLs, and authority revocation lists (which track revoked CA certificates).

The certificateRevocationList attribute contains CRLs as defined in RFC 2459. The authorityRevocationList attribute holds revocation information specifically for CA certificates. The optional deltaRevocationList contains incremental CRL updates for efficiency.

A related object class, deltaCRL, can be used to represent systems that use only delta CRLs without a base CRL.
sections.eli5: A CA can have a special folder in the directory for posting blacklists. It can keep the full list, or just updates, or both.

sections.title: Security Model
sections.content:
The schema does not require additional integrity protection because certificates and CRLs are digitally signed. An attacker cannot forge or modify a certificate in the directory without detection.

However, the RFC references RFC 2559 for security considerations regarding access control. Directory servers must protect who is allowed to query and modify PKI information. RFC 2119 requirement levels (MUST, SHOULD, etc.) are used to indicate which attributes must or may be included in PKI entries.
sections.eli5: The certificates are signed, so if someone messes with them in the directory, you can tell they're fake. But the server still needs to control who can read and change them.

references.text: Yeong, Y., Howes, T. and S. Kille, "Lightweight Directory Access Protocol", RFC 1777, March 1995.
Bradner, S., "Key Words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
